title: 38-70_United Auto Workers, Local 2322 v. University of Vermont
text:
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
UNITED AUTO WORKERS, )
LOCAL 2322 )
)
AND ) DOCKET NO. 23-43
)
THE UNIVERSITY OF VERMONT )
DECISION ON REMAND
On February 21, 2025, the Vermont Supreme Court reversed and remanded the February 20,
2024, Unit Determination Decision of the Vermont Labor Relations Board (“Board”) in which it
concluded that pre-doctoral fellows and trainees are employees for purposes of the State Employees
Labor Relations Act (SELRA), 3 V.S.A. §§ 901, 902. The University did not appeal, and the
Supreme Court did not review, the Board’s interpretation of the term “employee” under SELRA, nor
the Board’s specific factual findings and conclusions regarding graduate and research assistants,
other than to compare those findings with the lack of similar findings regarding pre-doctoral fellows
and trainees. The Supreme Court ruled that the Board decision lacked sufficient factual findings to
support the Board’s conclusion that pre-doctoral fellows and trainees are employees under SELRA.
The Supreme Court remanded the matter to the Board for further proceedings consistent with its
opinion.
On March 10, 2025, the Board Executive Director held a status conference with the parties to
determine whether they wished to file additional briefing on the issue remanded to the Board. The
parties agreed that they would provide targeted briefing on the issue. On April 10, 2025, the parties
filed with the Board final briefs and copies of the briefs they filed with the Vermont Supreme Court.
The Board has reviewed the transcripts, exhibits, and pleadings in this matter and issues its
remanded decision on the issue of the employee status of the pre-doctoral fellows and trainees. The
70

Board provides the following findings of fact, conclusions of law, and Order, and incorporates the
findings of fact from its February 20, 2024, decision.1
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. The University of Vermont (“University”) considers itself a research university and has been
striving to improve its ranking as a research university. Research universities are ranked
using the Carnegie classification, which classifies universities from very good research to no
research. At the time of the hearing, UVM was listed as an R-2, the middle ranking, with
hopes of moving up to an R-1 ranking.
2. The University benefits from the research conducted and the grants received by the
University, its faculty, and students.
3. The University receives about a quarter billion dollars or $250,000,000.00 in sponsored or
funded research grants. Of that amount approximately fifty percent is allotted to the
University towards sustaining its infrastructure.
4. The awarding organizations or agencies, like the National Institutes of Health, have
parameters for how the research funds will be spent. For the University to receive grants or
research funds, it must have personnel to perform the work of the research grant.
5. In recruiting Ph.D. students, the University competes with other universities nationally and
internationally. One of the tools it uses to distinguish itself and attract prospective students is
the overall financial support it offers students. The University makes its programs and the
1 The Supreme Court also identified confusion in the Board’s use of the term “assistantship(s)”
which the Board identified as referring to the entire group of approximately 627 graduate students
seeking membership in the proposed bargaining unit and the term “graduate assistantship” which the
Supreme Court interpreted as not applying to factual findings related to pre-doctoral fellows and
trainees. See Decision at n.1. To resolve any confusion, the Board will repeat findings that it
intended to also include pre-doctoral trainees and fellows.
71

accomplishments of its graduate students visible in the hopes of attracting graduate students
to the Graduate College.
6. A fellowship is a type of award or tool that the University uses to recruit the most
outstanding and diverse students. A fellowship is often awarded to bookend the Ph.D.
journey at the Graduate College.
7. The University offers two types of pre-doctoral fellowships depending on their source of
funding, either internal or external.
8. The source of funding for an internal fellowship is the University. A program, college, or the
University awards pre-doctoral fellowships directly to individual students on a merit and
competitive basis.
9. The source of funding for external fellowships are external or third party funding sources,
like the National Science Foundation or National Institutes of Health. With external funding
sources, the money flows through the University, which then distributes funds to the fellow.
10. Students are appointed as Predoctoral Trainees when their stipend is paid from a training
grant awarded to the University as opposed to the individual student. The University receives
the grant and pays the trainee from the grant.
11. Fellowships and traineeships may come with additional expectations, like mentoring and
networking. For example, the appointment letter awarded to Baxter Worthing includes the
requirement that they adhere to the requirements of the QuEST training grant. Union Exhibit
A.
12. Traineeships are designed to have additional expectations on the recipients that they
participate in specific experiences during their traineeship. For example, the appointment
letter awarded to Baxter Worthing includes the requirement that they adhere to the
72

requirements of the QuEST training grant. Union Exhibit A.
13. Fellowships may come with additional expectations, like mentoring and networking.
14. The amount of funds a student receives in a fellowship or traineeship (including stipend,
tuition scholarships and health insurance coverage) must be “at least equivalent to those
provided to GRAs and GTAs in the same program.” Employer Exhibit 13. Where the
program cannot provide equivalent funding, the program must figure out how to supplement
the funding to pay the fellow so that they are paid at least as much as the graduate or research
assistants.
Fellow and Trainees are employed by UVM
15. University publications and documents created to provide information to graduate
students, including pre-doctoral fellows and trainees, about their rights and
obligations refer to fellows and trainees as employees.
16. The Graduate College oversees pre-doctoral fellows and trainees. The UVM Guidelines
for Funded Graduate Students (“Guidelines”) govern graduate students in “work-based”
positions. The Guidelines apply to graduate students receiving funding as a “Graduate
Teaching Assistant, Graduate Assistant, Graduate Teaching/Research Assistant, or in a
Fellowship/Traineeship position.” Union Exhibit K.
17. The Guidelines establish an expected workload requirement to receive a full stipend.
18. The Guidelines provide that “[s]tudents receiving a full stipend devote, on average, .50
FTE effort (20 hours per week) to their teaching, research, or training duties during the
term of their appointment. The workload may vary.” Union Exhibit K. The Guidelines
also outline the holiday, sick leave, and time off policy.
73

19. The Graduate College determines the payment levels for stipends each year. Individual units
may alter the workload levels or stipend levels provided they are consistent with the
Guidelines.
20. According to the Guidelines, students funded by Assistantships, Fellowships or Traineeships
“may not work at UVM more than a total of .50 FTE or 20 hours per week” during the
academic year. Id.
21. The Guidelines also provide that students and their supervisors will provide notice to the
other about changes in duties, extra duties, and need for time off.
22. Fellows and trainees may lose their stipend or compensation if their performance is
inadequate or for gross negligence, dishonesty, or theft. Exhibit K.
23. The Guidelines outline the requirement for an annual appointment letter, setting forth the
term of appointment, salary, and any departmental conditions attached to the appointment.
24. The Graduate College reviews and approves appointment contracts between the
University and fellows and trainees.
25. The University sends an “Appointment Letter” to fellows and trainees outlining the
details of the positions offered through the Training Program or fellowship.
26. The details of the appointment letters are similar to those for research or graduate assistants.
27. The appointment letter outlines the length of the assignment, the stipend awarded, the
scholarship amounts awarded, health insurance coverage to be awarded, and the assigned
supervisor for the fellowship or training program.
28. The appointment letter provides that the fellowship and training grants are the only form of
“compensated effort” in which recipient students can engage without receiving permission
from the Graduate College.
74

29. Some appointment letters also detail when the first paycheck for academic year stipends will
be received. See Exhibit 17.
30. Fellows and trainees must complete an I-9 at the time of their initial appointment “to verify
they are either a U.S. Citizen or authorized to be employed in this country.” Exhibit 13.
31. The University advises graduate students that
Graduate students who are receiving any compensation for UVM employment
must, under immigration law, complete an Employment Eligibility Form known
as ‘I-9’before the end of their first day of employment.
Union Exhibit L.
32. The Graduate Student ePAR (electronic personnel action) contains instructions and
guidelines for completing the I-9 form. The instructions indicate that there are three sections
to the form, that “[n]ew employees and departments are responsible for sections 1 and 2.”
The system directs “employees” to fill out the first section. “Section 1 must be completed by
the employee no later than the first day of work.” Exhibit N.
33. In its Frequently Asked Questions for graduate students, the University explains when
payments or support to graduate students are taxable. The University recognizes support for
tuition and related expenses as not taxable because they do not represent compensation for
services. Exhibit L.
34. The University distinguishes non-compensable forms of support like tuition, from other
forms of support like living allowances, payments for travel or research, or internships which
“are potentially subject to income tax withholding and reporting.” Id.
35. The University also notifies its graduate students that “[c]compensation for teaching,
research, and/or other activities performed for the benefit of the University are also subject to
income tax withholding and reporting.” Exhibit L.
36. The University considers the pre-doctoral fellowship or training stipend to be taxable
75

income. Although it chooses not to withhold income taxes for the recipients and imposes this
obligation on the recipients.
37. Fellows and trainees are paid their stipend through the University payroll system, PeopleSoft.
38. Fellows and trainees, like other workers compensated for their services, must access the
“UVM Employee” pull down menu when accessing the PeopleSoft system. Union Exhibits
E, N.
39. The Biology Graduate Student Handbook for new graduate students, including fellows
and trainees, describes the following when answering the question about salary and
benefits:
First, review your contract letter, which contains important details
about your salary benefits as a graduate student. As a UVM
employee, your benefit and salary details are managed by the
PeopleSoft software package.
Union Exhibit Q (emphasis added).
40. Fellows and trainees are required to maintain a minimum GPA of 3.0 to continue to
participate in their fellowships or trainee programs.
41. The Graduate College resolves disputes regarding a failure to adhere to the terms and
requirements of a Fellowship or training grant. Exhibit 13.
Examples of Fellowship and Traineeships
42. Baxter Worthing (Plant Biology) and Bailey Kretzler (Plant and Soil Science) testified
about their experiences as fellows or trainees.
43. Baxter Worthing, a Ph.D. student in the Plant Biology Department of the College of Arts
and Sciences, has been enrolled continuously as a graduate student at UVM since the
76

fall 2018. He studies poplar trees and their ecological and economic benefits. Before
enrolling at UVM, Mr. Worthing obtained a master’s degree from Clark University in
2017. In the year between receiving his master’s and starting his Ph.D. studies at UVM,
Mr. Worthing worked as a lab technician for a biotech company in Boston.
44. During his first year, 2018-2019, Mr. Worthing was a pre-doctoral trainee through the
Quantitative and Evolutionary STEM Training (“QuEST”) program. As part of the
program, he was required to complete an internship outside of academia, participate in
training, and professional development seminars. The professional development
seminars involved providing feedback on the utility of professional development
seminars. To continue to receive the fellowship, he had to adhere to the specific
requirements of the QuEST program.
45. In 2020-2021, Mr. Worthing was a trainee under the QuEST program again because that
was the compensation vehicle offered to him. In this position, he worked on an applied
internship program at the Oakridge National Lab for the U.S. Department of Energy. He
received paychecks from UVM during the internship. He received a W-2 for the year he
was a QuEST trainee.
46. Bailey Kretzler, a Ph.D. student in the Department of Plant and Soil Science has been
enrolled continuously as a graduate student at UVM since 2020. She studies plant soil
microbe interactions in diversified agricultural systems, focusing on the plant soil
microbes in the three-system polyculture of corn, bean, and squash. She received her
Master of Science Degree at Lancaster University in the United Kingdom before starting
her doctoral program at UVM. She was admitted with three years of guaranteed funding.
77

She started her doctoral program in 2020 and during her first was a pre-doctoral trainee
through the National Science Foundation (“NSF”) QuEST program. The traineeship
provides a higher stipend level than the minimum stipend level for assistantships at
UVM.
47. As a trainee, she received tuition reimbursement and health insurance, like graduate
assistants. She was required to take training, complete an internship in a field outside
academia, interact with different disciplines, and participate in professional
development.
48. She was expected to work twenty hours a week on the traineeship. She had to adhere to
the specific requirements of the QuEST program to receive the funding. She was
supervised by her advisor and also program related faculty assisted in ensuring
compliance with the QuEST program.
49. In 2023-2024, Ms. Kretzler was “technically” a fellow. The compensation or funding
source was an internal fellowship with the Food Systems Research Center at UVM.
50. The work she performs as a fellow, and the supervision she receives, is the same as
when she was a research assistant.
51. Ms. Kretzler is compensated for her work as a fellow, which she accesses through the
PeopleSoft payment portal.
52. Ms. Kretzler is supervised in her work as a fellow. The entire time she has been at UVM,
including her time as a fellow, she has supported her advisor in the management of her
lab. She trains undergraduate students that come into the lab and facilitates lab meetings.
The lab management does not further her dissertation.
53. Ms. Kretzler uses the PeopleSoft program to facilitate her receipt of payment for her
78

fellowship. She used PeopleSoft as a graduate assistant and as a fellow. UVM paid her
through the program, and her payment was direct deposited. She received health
insurance through UVM but has to pay the premium.
54. The work performed through the fellowship or trainee is different from the aims and
goals of their academic programs.
55. Fellows and trainees are different from a scholarship or grant award because they
provide a service or benefit for the University. In exchange for this service or
benefit, the Fellows and trainees receive compensation in the form of a stipend.
56. The Fellows and Trainees perform the work assigned to them by a supervisor.
57. For the twenty hours of work or “effort” the fellows or trainees receive a stipend.
58. Fellows and trainees are regulated as employees under federal immigration laws, and
under federal and state tax laws.
MAJORITY OPINION
On remand, the Board reviews that portion of its decision in which it concluded that pre-
doctoral fellows and trainees are employees under the State Employees Labor Relations Act
(“SELRA”), 3 V.S.A. §§ 901, 902. Whether pre-doctoral fellows and trainees qualify or fit the
definition of employees under SELRA is relevant to whether they can be included in the proposed
employees seeking the right to self-organization and collective bargaining representation. See 3
V.S.A. §903(a). The Board, therefore, must determine whether pre-doctoral trainees and fellows are
employees under SELRA.
79

The applicable statute defines “employee” as a “State employee” that meets the definition of
section 902 (5), which provides as follows:
“State employee” means any individual employed on a permanent or
limited status basis by the state of Vermont, the Vermont State Colleges,
the University of Vermont, the State’s Attorneys’ offices, or as a full-time
deputy sheriff paid by the State pursuant to 24 V.S.A. § 290 (b), including
part-time employees, and an individual whose work has ceased as a
consequence of, or in connection with, any current labor dispute or
because of any unfair labor practice, but excluding and individual:
[subparagraphs (A) – (I) enumerated list of individuals excluded under the
statute]
. . . .
(J) determined after hearing by the Board, upon petition of any individual
desiring exclusion, of the employer, or of a collective bargaining unit, to
be in a position that is so inconsistent with the spirit and intent of the
chapter to warrant exclusion.
3 V.S.A. § 902 (5).
The statutory language is broad and defines employee to include “any individual
employed on a permanent or limited status basis” by the University of Vermont. Although
“employed” is not defined, the dictionary definition includes “to provide work to someone for pay.”
Heritage Dictionary (5thed. 2022). The United States Supreme Court, also referencing the dictionary,
provides the following definitions of “employee” in NLRB v. Town and Country, Electric, 516, U.S.
85 (1995):
The ordinary dictionary definition of employee includes “any person who works
for another in return for financial or other compensation.” Heritage Dictionary
604 (3d ed. 1992). See also Black’s Law Dictionary 525 (6th ed. 1990) (an
employee is a ‘person in the service of another under any contract of hire, express
or implied, oral or written, where the employer has the power or right to control
and direct the employee in the material details of how the work is to be
performed’).
80

The findings demonstrate that pre-doctoral fellows and trainees are under contract with the
University to perform services or effort on behalf of the University and the University has the power
or right to control them in material detail on how their work, service, or effort is performed. The
Graduate College monitors and issues an appointment letter to incoming pre-doctoral fellows and
trainees in which it lists the duration of service, the compensation to be awarded, the benefits to be
provided, the supervisor for the appointment, and the schedule for paychecks. The appointment
letter also limits and controls the labor of fellows and trainees by prohibiting them from engaging in
other “compensated effort at UVM.” Fellows and Trainees must sign the appointment letter to
indicate their acceptance of the appointment.
The University controls and limits the labor performed by the fellows and trainees. The
Graduate Guidelines detail the amount of labor or service fellows and trainees are expected to
perform to receive their stipend or compensation. The Guidelines prescribe that fellows and trainees
receiving full stipends, like other funded graduate students in “work based” positions, devote twenty
hours a week or .50 FTE effort to their duties. The Guidelines also outline the holiday, sick leave,
and time off policy. The Guidelines set out expectations that fellows and trainees will coordinate
with their supervisors about changes in duties, extra duties, and requests for time off. Fellows and
trainees can lose their stipends for insufficient work or for gross negligence or other forms of
misconduct.
Bailey Kretzler testified that with both her traineeship and fellowship she was required to
work twenty hours a week. Her supervisor directed and managed her work. The work she
performed as a fellow managing the lab and training undergraduates did not benefit her or her
dissertation.
81

The University admits through its own documents that fellows and trainees are
employees. The compensation the University provides to fellows and trainees is distributed
using the same payroll system as other UVM employees. “As a UVM employee, your benefit
and salary details are managed by the PeopleSoft Software package.” Union Exhibit Q.
Fellows and trainees, like other workers compensated for their services, must access the “UVM
Employee” drop down menu to access the payroll system and facilitate their payments. The
University materials explaining the I-9 form and process, use the term “employee” to describe
fellows and trainees who will receive compensation through payments from the University. In
its Frequently Asked Questions to Graduate Students, the University mandates that all
“[g]raduate students who are receiving any compensation for UVM employment must”
complete an I-9 “before the end of their first day of employment.” Exhibit L.
The University contends that fellows and trainees should not be considered employees
because, unlike graduate or research assistants, their funding source is portable which affords them
greater flexibility and discretion. This argument relies on a faulty premise and is otherwise not
persuasive. The traineeships and internal fellowships are funded through research funds awarded to
and distributed by the University. Indeed, the source of funding for Ms. Kretzler’s fellowship is the
Food Systems Research Center at UVM. The University controls the funding mechanism or source
of income for the trainees and internal fellows. The funds available through an external fellowship
are still administered by, or “flow through,” the University. The University monitors the fellows,
can remove them for inadequate performance, and applying the Graduate Guidelines expects from
them .50 FTE or twenty hours of effort each week. The University also benefits from the fellows
receiving external funds and working on projects and research that enhances the University and its
Carnegie classification.
82

The fellows and trainees are compensated for the service or work they perform for the benefit
of the University. The University receives 250 million dollars a year in research grants. One half of
that amount is retained by the University itself to sustain its infrastructure or operation of the
University and does not fund the research or students performing the research. Graduate students,
including fellows and trainees, supply the labor to perform the research required to receive and the
deliverables expected through these grants. The University benefits from the amount of funds it
acquires through research grants and at the time of the hearing it expected to attain the coveted R-1
Carnegie ranking because of this benefit.
The University distinguishes between financial support that primarily benefits the student
from financial support for service or effort that benefits the University. According to the
University’s own document, where the work or service performed by the graduate student benefits
the University, the compensation received for that effort is taxable. The University treats fellowship
and trainee compensation as taxable income. Fellows and trainees are compensated for the service,
work, or benefit provided to the University and their income is taxed.
The provisions of SELRA are sufficiently broad to include pre-doctoral fellows and trainees.
Fellows and trainees are employees as that term is used in SELRA. Fellows and trainees perform
service or work for the benefit of the University for which they are compensated. They are
“individuals” employed by the University of Vermont and fall within the jurisdiction of the Board.
The material similarities between fellows and trainees and teaching and graduate assistants
further supports that the former funded positions fit within the definition of “employee” under
SELRA. Any differences, like being denied a W-2, are not material or distinguishable when
evaluating employee status under SELRA. That the University imposes on fellows and trainees the
83

administrative burden of calculating their own withholding taxes does not disqualify them as
employees under SELRA.
Like research and teaching assistants, trainees and fellows cannot engage in additional
compensated effort at UVM without permission from the Graduate College. The Graduate College
oversees and administers appointment letters to both groups that outline the terms and conditions of
service, compensation, and benefits. The number of hours expected of fellows and trainees is
outlined in the Guidelines. Like graduate and research assistants, fellows and trainees must
complete an I-9 form before the “end of their first day of employment” to demonstrate they are
“authorized to be employed in this country.” Both groups can lose their compensation or positions
for poor performance or conduct. Both groups are directed by their supervisors in the performance
of their work or service. Fellows and trainees are compensated by and receive a paycheck from the
employee payroll system PeopleSoft.
As Ms. Kretzler testified, the work she performed and the supervision she received as a
fellow was the same as when she was a research assistant. Indeed, during her last year, her funding
source was a fellowship, but she performed the same role as she had the prior year as a research
assistant. Her supervisor was the same and directed her in her work.
Pre-doctoral fellows and trainees provide a service, work, effort, or benefit to the University
for which they are compensated or paid by the University and are supervised or monitored in
performance of such efforts.
84

The Board finds that the following is an appropriate bargaining unit:
All full-time and regular part-time graduate teaching assistants, graduate research
assistants, graduate assistants, and pre-doctoral trainees, pre-doctoral trainees/fellows,
and all other graduate students in other titles employed in an academic position.
Dated this 9th day of September 2025, at Montpelier, Vermont.
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
/s/ David Boulanger
David Boulanger, Acting Chair
/s/ Robert Greemore
Robert Greemore
85

DISSENTING OPINION
With all due respect, I disagree with the opinion of the majority on the application of the
exclusion provision of Section 902 (5) (J).
The positions in the proposed bargaining are so inconsistent with the spirit and intent of
the State Employees Labor Relations Act as to warrant exclusion. 902(5)(J). All of the positions
in the proposed bargaining unit are students and must remain as students to continue to receive
stipends and fellowships. The services the graduate assistants or fellows provide are in the
context of their role as students.
The relationship between the graduate assistants and UVM is primarily that of student-
teacher, with an educational rather than economic focus. The positions are fully integrated into
their academic programs. The rights and obligations that attach through SELRA are not
compatible with the overarching educational relationship between the University and students.
/s/ Alan Willard
Alan Willard
86
